reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Jade is learning something new. What Jade is learning: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing.
story:
Jade sat near the big red truck. Her friend Tom had it first. He pushed it across the rug. Vroom, vroom.

Jade wanted the truck now. She grabbed it with both hands. Tom held on too. The truck stopped rolling. It did not go anywhere at all.

Jade let go. "The truck stops when we both pull," she said. Tom blinked at her. "Then it goes when one hand lets go?" he asked. Jade nodded. "You first. I will count."

Tom drove the truck to the toy barn. Jade counted to ten. Then he gave it back. Jade filled the truck with little hay bales, one by one. She drove it back to Tom. He counted to ten, very slow, to make her giggle.

Then Tom's cat jumped in the truck bed. It sat on all the hay. Tom laughed so hard he fell over. Jade picked up the cat. "Cats do not wait for turns," she said.

Tom drove the cat around the rug twice.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Wren sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
story:
Wren went to the store with Dad. She wanted a book about trucks. She found one on a shelf.

"Can this book come home with us?" she asked.

"Not today," said Dad. "But look, there is a library next door. At the library, you can borrow books and take them home."

Wren picked a truck book. It had words on every page. Dad pointed at a word. "That says truck," he said. Wren laughed. "Words can talk!"

At the desk, a lady stamped the book. "Bring it back soon," she said. "Then other kids can read it too."

Wren hugged the book. "It is mine forever!"

"Not forever," said the lady. "Just for now."

Wren opened the book. She turned page one, then page two, all the way to the end. Then she started again.

"Tomorrow," said Wren, "the book goes back. But first, one more truck."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Logan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them.
story:
Logan waited at the bus stop with Mama. The sun was out. It was sunny and hot. Logan took off his hat and fanned his face.

Then the wind came. It was windy! Logan's hat went up, up, up. "My hat is lost!" he said. The hat did not roll far. It blew behind the bench. Logan ran and got it. "The wind pushed my hat," he said. He put it back on his head.

Big clouds came next. Rain fell. It was rainy! Mama opened her umbrella. Ping, ping went the rain on top. "The rain can't get my toe," said Logan. His shoe kept it dry. Then the bus came. "Warm bus," said Logan. He climbed in and smiled at his hat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Xavier is learning to swim at the local pool.
story:
Xavier went to the pool with his dad. The water was blue and cool. His teacher, Miss Ana, said, "Hold my hands." Xavier held on tight.

"Kick your legs," said Miss Ana. "Kick, kick, kick." Xavier kicked his legs. His little feet hit the water. Splish, splash! The water jumped up everywhere. Drops fell on his nose.

Then Xavier felt something. His kicking made him move. He kicked fast and went far. He kicked slow and stayed still. Kick, kick, kick, and off he went, like a little boat across the pool. "I moved!" said Xavier. "You moved!" said Miss Ana. She clapped her hands. Dad clapped too.

After swimming, Xavier was hungry. He sat with Dad at the table. Dad gave him a fork and some noodles. Xavier took a quick bite. "The noodles live in my tummy now," he said with a giggle. Dad laughed and gave him a big towel hug. "Swim again next week?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Xavier. "Kick, kick, kick!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Arya sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
story:
Arya wanted her teddy bear at bedtime. She could not find him. "I will look now," she said.

She looked under the bed. She looked in the toy box. No teddy. Arya remembered yesterday. Yesterday she took teddy in the car. They went to the town. They went to the big shop. The bag was so heavy, and Mommy had to help carry it. "Maybe teddy is in the car," Arya said. It is still there now, she thought.

Mommy took her hand. They walked out in the dark. Mommy opened the car door. There was teddy, sitting on the seat! Arya hugged him. "You stayed here after yesterday," she said. "Now you can come to bed."

Mommy smiled. "We will look first, next time," she said. Arya nodded. "Tomorrow I will hold you tight," she told teddy. "I will hold you tight all night." She climbed into bed. She pulled the blanket up. She held teddy tight. "Night night, teddy," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Charles is learning something new. What Charles is learning: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet.
story:
Charles wanted his sandwich now. He ran to the table and grabbed it.

"Stop," said Grandma. "Your hands are dirty." Charles looked at his hands. He saw mud on his fingers. "Why can't I eat?" he asked. Grandma held up two fingers. "Twenty seconds with soap. Then you can eat."

Charles sighed. He hurried to the sink. He pumped the soap. He rubbed his hands together. One, two, three. He kept counting. The bubbles grew big and white. "Look, a bubble beard!" he said. Grandma laughed. "You look like Santa."

At fifteen, the bubbles popped. At twenty, he rinsed. The mud went down the drain. "The soap took the mud away," Charles said. "Yes it did," said Grandma. "Now the sandwich." Charles took a big bite of his sandwich. "Yum. Clean hands taste good too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Ibrahim is learning something new. What Ibrahim is learning: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more.
story:
Ibrahim was at Grandma's house. Grandma had baked cookies. She put them on two flat plates.

"One plate is for you," said Grandma. "One plate is for Grandpa."

Ibrahim wanted the plate with more cookies. But which one had more? He had to know.

He counted his plate. He touched each cookie. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. The last number was five. So there were five cookies.

Grandpa laughed. "Count them from the other side too," he said.

Ibrahim reached over and touched the far cookie first. "One, two, three, four, five." It was five again!

"I counted from the other end," said Ibrahim. "It is still five!"

Then he counted Grandpa's plate. "One, two, three, four." Four cookies.

"Mine has more!" said Ibrahim. "Five is more than four."

Grandma smiled. "Grandpa is not hungry," she said. "It is almost dinner."

Just then Grandpa pushed his plate across the table. "You can have my four too," he said.

Ibrahim counted them all together. "Nine cookies!" he said.

Grandma put one more on his plate. "Now it is ten," she said. "The very last number."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Rowan is welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family.
story:
Rowan ran down the long hall. His mama had a new baby. A tiny baby brother. Rowan wanted to hold him right away.

But the baby was asleep. "New babies sleep a lot," Mama whispered. "He wakes up when his tummy is full. Then we can hold him." So Rowan sat down on a chair by the bed.

Rowan began to count. "One, two, three." The baby slept. "Four, five, six." The baby slept. Rain tapped on the window like a little storm. "Seven, eight, nine, ten," Rowan counted, slow and quiet. Still the baby slept. So Rowan counted again.

Then the baby made a small cry. His eyes opened. "His tummy woke him up," Rowan said. A nurse helped feed him. The baby drank and drank until his tummy was full.

Now it was time. Rowan sat very still on the big bed. The nurse put the baby in his arms. "Hello, baby brother," Rowan said. "I counted to ten two times. Now you are awake." The baby grabbed Rowan's finger and held on tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Charlotte is learning something new. What Charlotte is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
story:
Charlotte was at Ben's house. Mommy made warm toast for snack. Charlotte wanted to spread the butter all by herself.

"Slow and steady," said Ben's mommy. "Slow and steady."

Charlotte held the knife. She spread the butter. The warm toast made the butter soft, so it slid on smooth. "One, two, three strokes," said Charlotte. The toast was covered.

Then came the milk. Charlotte poured too fast the first time. Milk splashed onto the table. "We can wash the table," said Ben. He got a cloth.

Charlotte looked at the cup. She made her hand tight around the pitcher. She poured a little bit, then a little bit more. "One, two, three," said Charlotte. "Stop before the top!"

The milk went up to the line on the cup. Not one drop spilled.

"Slow and steady," said Charlotte. She took a big bite of toast and a big drink of milk.

"Want to play in the yard now?" asked Ben.

"Yes," said Charlotte. "I will bring my cup. I will hold it tight."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Henri is learning something new. What Henri is learning: to draw a map of their bedroom or classroom with a key showing where each thing is.
story:
Henri wanted to draw a map of his room. But he did not know where to start.

"Start with your bed," Mama said. "Put a bed in the middle of your paper."

Henri drew a small bed. He put it in the middle. Then he drew his toy box. He drew his rug. Soon his paper was full of little shapes.

Papa came to look. "Is this little square the rug?" he asked.

Henri looked at his paper. He could not tell. The square could be the rug. It could also be the door.

So Henri made a key. He drew a tiny square at the bottom. He drew a rug next to it. Now the square said "rug."

He drew a tiny circle. He drew a bed next to it. Now the circle said "bed."

Papa pointed to a shape. "What is this one?"

Henri checked his key. "That is my toy box!" he said.

Mama gave him a warm hug. "Your map helps us find things," she said.

Henri smiled. He drew one more shape. He drew a little star. The star showed his favorite spot, right next to the window.

Papa traced the map with his finger. "I follow the star," he said. He walked to the window and sat down.

"Welcome to my spot," said Henri.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Jake is attending a religious or cultural celebration with family.
story:
Jake ran into Grandma's house. Tonight was the big family party!

Grandpa was lighting candles at the table. Jake wanted to help. "Not with matches," said Grandpa. "Matches are for me." Grandpa lit each candle, one by one.

But then the wind from the window blew. One little candle went out! The flame was gone. Jake felt sad. The party needed all the candles lit.

Jake had an idea. He pushed the window shut with his hand. Now the wind could not come in.

"Look, Grandpa!" said Jake. Grandpa lit the candle again. The flame stayed up tall. It did not go out this time.

All the candles were shining. The family sang together. Jake clapped and sang too.

Grandpa gave Jake a big smile. "You fixed it," he said. "You kept our candles safe."

Jake sat close to Grandma. He watched the flames dance. Not one went out again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Arthur is searching for a lost favorite toy.
story:
Arthur went to the grocery store with Mom. He held his little toy dog. The dog was his favorite. But when they got to the apples, Arthur looked down. His hands were empty. The dog was gone.

"Where did you go first?" asked Mom. Arthur thought hard. "The bread aisle," he said. "We got bread first." So they walked back the way they came. They passed the big cans of paint. A man was painting a wall blue. Arthur kept looking. They passed the milk. Then Arthur saw something on the floor by the bread. It was his little dog!

Arthur picked it up and hugged it tight. He squeezed the dog's tummy. "Woof, woof," barked the dog. Arthur laughed. "You were waiting by the bread," he said. "We came back and we found you." Mom smiled and kissed his head. Arthur held the dog all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Emma sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
story:
Emma went to the library with her toy owl. The owl was smelly from playing in the mud. Emma wanted a book to share with him. The owl book was on a high shelf. Emma was too small to reach it.

She found a big ball on the rug. The ball was a circle. Emma put a block on top of the ball. The block fell off. The circle rolled away. Emma tried again. The circle rolled away again.

Then Emma found some books. The books were rectangles. They had flat sides. Emma stacked one rectangle on another rectangle. The stack did not fall. It grew tall like a tower. Emma stood on her toes and reached up high. She got the owl book.

Emma hugged the smelly owl. "The circle rolled," she said. "The rectangles did not." The librarian smiled. "Time to read," said Emma.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Penelope is learning something new. What Penelope is learning: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name.
story: Penelope sat at the little table. She wanted to write her name. She held her pencil in her whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. The P looked like a squashed bug. She frowned at the paper. "Why is my P so messy?" she asked. Her friend Tomo looked over. "Watch me," he said. Tomo pinched the pencil with two fingers. Then he let it rest on one more finger. Penelope tried it. She pinched with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil sat on her middle finger, like a coin resting on a shelf. Now the pencil did not fly out of her hand. She wrote P. Then E. Then N. The letters stood up straight, like tall soldiers. "My pencil listens now," she said. At snack time, she ate her salty crackers and smiled. Then she wrote her whole name again, just to see it. "P-E-N-E-L-O-P-E," she read out loud, and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Everly sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
story:
Everly wanted to build a barn at daycare. The toy farm animals needed a home. She found some squishy red balls and stacked them up. The balls rolled off. The barn fell down. "Oh no," said Everly.

Her friend Milo was sad too. His cow had no home. Everly wanted to help him. She looked at the block shelf. She pulled out a block with four flat sides. It had four sides the same, like a window. It did not roll. She stacked more of these squares. The wall stood tall.

Then she found a block with three sides. It made a pointy roof. She put it on top. "The barn is done," she said. Milo put his cow inside. Everly put her pig next to it. The pig oinked.

"The balls rolled because they are round," said Everly. "These blocks stay because they are flat." Milo clapped his hands. "Square wall, triangle roof," he said. Everly patted the squishy pig. "Night night, pig," she said. "Your farm house is warm."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Florence is learning something new. What Florence is learning: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands.
story:
Florence stood at the big baseball diamond. Papa had set a hoop on the grass. He gave her a small red beanbag.

"Throw it in the hoop," said Papa. Florence threw the beanbag. It hit the net and fell out. It bounced on the grass. She tried again. It fell out again.

Florence looked at her hands. What if she held the beanbag up high? She lifted her arms and let it drop. The beanbag went straight down into the hoop. Papa clapped. When she threw from up high, it went in. When she threw from down low, it did not.

Then Papa rolled her a big blue ball. It bumped her arm and rolled away. She tried one hand. It bounced off her fingers. Florence held out both hands, like a big bowl. The ball landed right in them. Both hands caught it. One hand did not.

Florence threw the beanbag high into the hoop. Then she caught the ball with both hands. She did it again and again. The red beanbag went in, and the blue ball stayed put.

"Watch me, Papa!" she called. Papa picked up a stick and drew a star in the dirt. Florence put her hands on her hips like a dancer. "Am I a star too?" she asked. "You are," said Papa, and he tossed her the ball one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Connor sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited.
story:
Connor sat on his bed. Outside, rain tapped on his window. "It is wet today," he said. "We cannot go to the park." His tummy felt heavy and his mouth turned down. He was sad.

He sat for a while. Then he got his paper and paints. He painted a big yellow sun. He painted the swings at the park. He painted himself on a swing, going high. His arms began to move fast. He was excited now!

"Where did my sad go?" he asked himself. He thought about it. "The sad went away when I painted the sun." His face felt light and his mouth turned up. He was happy.

Later, Dad came in. "The rain stopped," said Dad. "Do you want to go now?"

"Yes!" said Connor. He jumped off the bed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Mateo sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
story:
Mateo ran to the park. He saw the big slide first. A girl was already at the ladder.

"Can I go too?" asked Mateo.

"You can go after me," said the girl. "One at a time."

Mateo waited. He watched her climb up. Then she slid down, fast. She laughed at the bottom.

Now it was his turn. Mateo climbed up, up, up. He slid down, fast too. "Whee!" he said.

Then the girl came back. She stood behind him. "Your turn again," said Mateo.

They took turns, over and over. The line got longer. A small boy joined, then a big kid. Everyone waited at the ladder. Nobody pushed. Everyone slid.

Then the girl held out a stick. "Want to chase the ball with me?" she said. The ball rolled into the dark shade under the tree. Mateo took the stick. They chased the ball together. They shared the stick, one at a time.

"Same time tomorrow?" said the girl.

"Yes," said Mateo. He waved all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Noah is starting the first day of school.
story:
Noah stood at the door of his classroom. He held his teddy bear tight. He wanted to sit next to the other kids, but his feet would not move.

Then Noah saw a girl crying. Her name was Mia. She looked lost in the big room. Noah walked over and held out his teddy. "You can hug him," Noah said. Mia hugged the bear and smiled.

The teacher put blocks on the carpet. Noah stacked one block on top of another. Then he added more. The blocks made a big square tower. Mia put one block on the top too. Now the tower was taller.

"Come play," said Mia. Noah sat down next to her. He did not hold the teddy anymore. His hands were busy with blocks. "School is fun," said Mia. Noah smiled and put one more block on the tower.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Mason sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
story:
Mason ran into the library. He held his lunch bag tight. Inside was his sandwich in a box. But then the bag tipped over. The lid popped off and rolled away. "Come back!" said Mason.

The lid was a circle. Circles can roll. It rolled past the big square rug. It rolled past a stack of square books. The books did not roll. Squares have flat sides. They stay still. The lid stopped by a tall rectangle door.

Mason looked up. A triangle sign hung on the wall. Its tip pointed to the warm reading corner. Mason ran there. He found his lid next to the warm radiator. He clicked it back on his sandwich box. "Circles roll, squares stay," said Mason. He hugged his box and sat down to read.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Levi is spending a surprise snow day at home.
story: Levi woke up and saw white everywhere. "No school today!" said Mom. "It is a snow day." Levi put on his boots. He walked next door to Mr. Kim's house. His foot went crunch, crunch on the snow. Mr. Kim was sprinkling salt on his walkway. "Why do you do that?" Levi asked. "Watch and see," said Mr. Kim. Levi sat on the step. He watched the little salt bits. The snow near them got small and wet. Soon there were dark spots on the walk. "The salt makes the snow melt!" said Levi. "Yes. That is why I shop for big bags of salt every winter." Then Mr. Kim gave Levi a juicy orange. Levi ate it and watched the white walk turn gray, one wet spot at a time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Claire sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Claire sat in her big car seat. She held her white teddy bear. His name was Mr. Buttons.

The car went over a bump. Mr. Buttons fell down. He slid under the front seat. Claire could not reach him.

Claire tried and tried. Her arm was too short. She wanted to cry. But she had another idea.

"Daddy, please stop the car," she said. "Please help me. Mr. Buttons is lost."

Dad looked in the mirror. He found a safe spot. The car stopped.

Dad reached under the seat. Out came Mr. Buttons! One small rip showed on his leg.

"Thank you, Daddy!" said Claire. She hugged the bear tight.

Then she looked at the rip. "Mr. Buttons fell because of the bump," she said. "He got hurt because he fell."

Dad smiled. "We can sew his leg at home," he said. "We will ask Mom to help too."

Claire held up the bear. "Say thank you, Mr. Buttons," she whispered.

The car drove on. Claire waved at a white cloud out the window. "Look, Daddy! A sheep in the sky!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Oliver is reading a whole book alone for the first time.
story:
Oliver was at Grandma's house. He found a small book on the big chair. "I will read it all by myself," he said. Grandma sat near him in the sunny room.

Oliver pointed at the first word. He said it out loud. Then he said the next word. Then the next one. One word, two words, three words. His finger slid under each word like a little train.

The words made a sentence. The sentence made a page. He turned the page. "Cat," he read. "Pink cat." The pink cat sat on a hat. He laughed and turned another page.

At the last page, the pink cat had kittens. One, two, three small kittens. Oliver did not know they were coming. "Grandma, look!" he yelled. "Babies!" Grandma clapped her hands. Oliver held the book up high. Then he ran to the shelf to find one more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Arya sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
story:
Arya wanted to see the moon. But it was bedtime, and the moon was not up yet. "The moon comes later," said Mama. Arya pouted. She did not want to wait for later.

"Yesterday the moon was big," said Arya. "Today it is hiding." Mama smiled. "Let's look now," she said. They looked out the window together. They saw only stars. The stars twinkled like tiny lamps.

Mama had an idea. "Let's bake muffins for tomorrow," she said. Arya helped from her stool. She poured the heavy bag of flour. Mama stirred. "Tomorrow we will meet Papa at the bus stop in town," said Mama. "We will bring him a warm muffin."

Arya put on her pajamas. She brushed her teeth. Then Mama called, "Quick! Look now!" Arya ran to the window. There was the moon, round and bright. It had come out while they baked. Arya waved at it. "Good night, moon," she said. "I will see you tomorrow too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Sophia is learning something new. What Sophia is learning: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour.
story:
Sophia sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a big orange pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. Not one drop.

Teacher Maya put out three cups. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. Sophia tapped her ear. "Say them with me," said Teacher Maya. "Red, yellow, blue!" Sophia said. They said it two more times. Red, yellow, blue!

Sophia dipped her brush in red. She made a red circle on the paper. Then she dipped in yellow. She painted yellow right on top. She held her breath.

The red spot turned orange. Bright, cool, pumpkin orange! "It changed!" said Sophia. "My paint made a magic colour."

She painted the big pumpkin. "One pumpkin," she counted. "Two pumpkins. Three pumpkins." All of them stayed orange on the paper.

Teacher Maya smiled. "Try two more colours," she said. Sophia looked at blue. She looked at yellow. She put her brush in the blue.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Arthur is searching for a lost favorite toy.
story:
Arthur lost his favorite dinosaur at daycare. He looked in the toy box. No dinosaur. He looked under the table. No dinosaur.

His friend Mia said, "Where did you play with him last?" Arthur thought hard. "The paint table!" He ran to the paint table. He saw red paint, blue paint, and green paint. He saw paint on his own hands. Then he saw paint on the chair. And there was his dinosaur, hiding behind the chair!

"He was where I left him," said Arthur. "Dinosaurs stay where we play!" Mia clapped her hands. Arthur let Mia share the dinosaur. They made him stomp in the paint. One, two, three stomps. Green footprints went across the paper.

At nap time, Arthur put his favorite dinosaur right next to his mat. "Stay here, friend," he whispered. The dinosaur stayed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Lucy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Lucy sat at the dinner table. There was thick spaghetti on her plate. One long piece looked just like a wiggly worm.

Lucy saw the bread. She wanted the bread. It was far away from her. She reached and reached. She said, "Bread!" Papa did not pass it. She said, "Bread, now!" Papa still did not pass it. Lucy frowned. Why did the bread not come?

Mama leaned close. "Try the little word," said Mama. Lucy thought hard. Then she said, "Bread, please." Papa passed the bread right away. "Thank you," said Lucy. She took a big bite. "The bread came because I said please!" she said.

Then Lucy reached for her milk. The cup tipped over. Milk went splash, all over the table. "Sorry, Mama," said Lucy. "It was too far." "That is okay," said Mama. "When it is too far, call for help." So when Lucy wanted the apple slices, she did not reach. She called out, "Help, please!" Mama slid the apples close to her. "Thank you," said Lucy again. She slurped up the long worm piece of spaghetti. "Please works," said Lucy. Papa laughed. "Yes, it does."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Zoe sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
story:
Zoe wanted to help Grandma bake cookies. "First we look," said Grandma. Zoe used her eyes to see the flour, white and soft in the cup. Then Grandma said, "Now listen." Zoe used her ears. The mixer went whir, whir, whir.

"I smell them!" said Zoe. The cookies were in the oven, and Grandma did the hot part. Zoe used her nose to smell the sweet, warm cookies. She waited. She counted, "One, two, three." She waited some more.

At last the cookies were cool. Zoe touched one with her finger. It felt bumpy. She took a little bite. Her tongue tasted sugar and butter. "How many things helped you?" asked Grandma. Zoe counted on her fingers. "Eyes, ears, nose, fingers, tongue. Five!" Grandma smiled. "What a lucky girl," she said. Zoe took one more big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Gabriel sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
story:
Gabriel ran into the garden. "A bird! A bird!" he shouted. The bird sat in the tree. Then it flew down to the ground. It hopped. It pecked. It pulled a worm out of the dirt. "He found his food!" said Gabriel.

Gabriel looked for more birds. He saw a small one by the fence. It did not hop. It just sat there. It looked small and still. "Are you hungry?" Gabriel asked. "Where is your food?" The bird fluffed its feathers. It stayed on the ground.

Gabriel ran to get Grandpa. "Come fast!" he said. Grandpa brought a little cup of seeds. He set it down near the fence. The small bird looked. Then the small bird hopped to the cup. It pecked the seeds. Peck, peck, peck. "She is eating!" said Gabriel. "She is eating!"

Grandpa filled a low dish with water too. The bird drank. Then she flew up into the tree. She sat on a branch in the bright sun. "Now she has food," said Gabriel. "Now she has water. And the tree is her house!"

Grandpa laughed. "You are a good helper." Gabriel clapped his hands. The bird sang from the tree. Gabriel sang back, "Tweet, tweet, tweet!" A car went by on the road. Gabriel shut the gate to keep the garden safe and quiet. Then he sat on the step and watched his new friend.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Emma sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
story:
Emma went to the library with Dad. She wanted to find a book about owls. "Where is the owl book?" she asked.

Dad said, "Look at the signs. Each shape points the way." Emma looked up. A red circle hung over the picture books. She walked under the circle. She found a book with a round moon. No owls there.

She tried again. A blue square hung over the toy corner. No owls there either. She kept looking. A green triangle hung over the animal books. Emma walked under the triangle. There was an owl book! The owl had big round eyes and a triangle beak.

Emma hugged the book. "I found it!" she said. Dad smiled. They sat at the long rectangle table to read. Emma turned the square pages one by one. "This owl looks like my triangle," she said. Dad laughed. "Let's share it with baby brother tonight."

Emma checked out her book. She waved to the owl on the cover. "Bye, owl," she said. "See you at home."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Naomi is learning something new. What Naomi is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
story:
Rain fell on the windows of the shop. It was a quiet day, so Papa said, "Come, I will teach you something new."

He gave Naomi a small tablet. "Hold the round button down," he said. Naomi pressed it. The screen stayed black. "You have to hold it," said Papa. So she held it and held it. Then the screen lit up! "I did it!" she shouted.

Next, Papa showed her a blue square. Naomi tapped it. The drawing app opened. She drew a cat with rain in the picture. She drew a small red sun too.

"Time to put it away," said Papa. Naomi pressed the button again and held it. The screen went dark. "I held it down, so it slept," she said. Then she slid the tablet into the drawer.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Romy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
story:
Romy looked at the cage. The class bunny, Pip, sat very still. "Pip is hungry," said Romy. She found a carrot in the toy box. It was orange and soft. She put it in the cage. Pip sniffed it. Pip did not eat it. "Oh no," said Romy.

Teacher Mia came over. She held a real carrot from the snack table. She took a small knife and cut it into short pieces. "Real food, not a toy," said Teacher Mia. Romy put a piece in the cage. Pip grabbed it with his teeth. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

Outside the window, a bird flew by with a twig. It was building a nest in the big tree. "Look, Pip," said Romy. "The bird gets real sticks." Pip kept crunching. Then he hopped close and rubbed his nose on her hand. "You like real carrots best," said Romy. Pip's ears wiggled up and down.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Hailey is attending a religious or cultural celebration with family.
story:
Hailey put on her new dress for Diwali. It had little gold flowers on it. The dress felt itchy, so Mama helped her put on a soft shirt under it.

Hailey wanted to help light the diyas. Mama lit the little lamps with a match. Hailey watched from her spot on the pillow. She could not touch the fire. But Mama said she could place the diyas on the sill.

Hailey set one clay lamp down by the window. The light made a shiny spot on the wall. Then she set another lamp next to it. Now there were two shiny spots. Hailey clapped her hands.

Papa came in with sweets. "Look," said Hailey. She moved one lamp a little. The shiny spot on the wall moved too. Papa laughed and clapped with her. "Happy Diwali, Hailey," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Caleb is learning something new. What Caleb is learning: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more.
story:
Caleb sat at the little red table at the tutoring centre. Miss Priya put down two bowls of blocks. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Caleb counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." He wanted to check. So he counted the other way, from the last block back. "One, two, three, four, five."

He sat very still. "It is five both ways!" Miss Priya laughed. "Counting is a cool trick like that."

Then he counted the red bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven! "The red bowl has more," said Caleb. "Seven is more than five."

The idea stuck in his head like glue. He counted his crackers at snack time too. "One, two, three." He counted them backwards. "One, two, three." Still three!

"Miss Priya!" he called. "My crackers agree with each other!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Eleanor is learning something new. What Eleanor is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
story:
Eleanor wanted toast and milk. She wanted to make it all by herself. Mom said, "You can try."

Eleanor took the butter from the fridge. The butter was cold and hard. She pushed it on the toast. The toast tore. Big holes showed up. Mom got out a new bowl of soft butter. Mom said, "We buy this soft kind now." Eleanor dipped her knife. The soft butter slid on. It covered the toast like paint.

Next came the milk. Eleanor held the jug far above the cup. Milk splashed out. A puddle grew on the table. Then she set the jug lip right at the cup's edge. She tipped it slowly. The milk went in, not out.

"The soft butter works," said Eleanor. "And I poured it slow, up close."

Mom wiped the puddle and gave her a smile. "Not a lazy try at all," said Mom. Eleanor bit her toast and drank her milk. "More please," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Luna is learning something new. What Luna is learning: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal.
story:
Luna held a warm bun at the festival. It smelled sweet, like honey. Grandma said, "Wait. We say our blessing first."

Luna was hungry. She took a big bite anyway. Then everyone joined hands. They said the words together. Luna's mouth was too full. She could not say them. She felt sad, but Grandma just smiled and patted her back.

At the next table, a woman wore a hat with a long red feather. The feather bobbed low when she bowed her head. "She is getting ready too," said Grandma. "See how everyone stops first? The food waits until the words are done."

Luna watched. Because everyone said the words together, the big table got quiet and calm. Then everyone ate at the same time.

A new plate of buns came. This time Luna set her bun down. She dug her fingers into Grandma's hand and her aunt's hand too. She bowed her head. "Bless this food and all who share it," said Luna, clear and loud. Everyone smiled at her.

"Now we eat," said Grandma. Luna took her bite and the bun tasted even better.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Dylan is cooking or baking a meal for the family.
story:
Dylan went to the store with Dad. "We need eggs," said Dad. "And it is your job to hold them." Dylan was brave. He asked a worker, "Where are the eggs, please?" The worker smiled and pointed. "Aisle two, little chef."

Dylan wanted big, tall pancakes for the family. Dad held up a small box. "This is baking soda. We need it too." "Why?" asked Dylan. "You will see," said Dad, with a grin.

At home, Dylan helped wash the apples for the fruit bowl. Then he poured buttermilk into the bowl. Dad added the baking soda. The batter went fizz, fizz, fizz. Little bubbles popped up everywhere. "The bubbles came because of the baking soda!" said Dylan. Dad poured the batter into the pan. The pancake grew and grew. It puffed up like a tall hat. "It is bigger than my plate!" said Dylan. His sister popped a berry on top and said, "Now it wears a hat too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Beau sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
story:
Beau had a library book. It was about a big green turtle. The turtle could swim and fish for food. Beau loved that turtle.

Beau opened the book. He turned the pages one by one. First page, then next page, then the last page. The pictures told him what to do. The words did too. "Those words say swim," said Mama. Beau pointed at the words. He made his arms swim like the turtle.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Beau. He held it tight.

"No," said Mama. "We take it back on Tuesday. Then another kid can read it too."

Beau felt sad. But he had a strong idea. He asked Mama for paper. He drew the turtle. He drew the fish. He drew the waves. He asked Mama to write the word turtle. She wrote it big.

On Tuesday, Beau carried the book to the library. He put it in the return box. It went down with a whoosh. Then a girl picked up the turtle book. She hugged it tight, just like Beau had.

Beau smiled. He held his own paper book. "My turtle stays with me," he said. He turned to page one.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Charlie is going to the dentist for the first time.
story:
Charlie held Mom's hand at the bus stop. "The bus will take us to the dentist!" said Mom. Charlie jumped up and down. He was not late. The big bus came. Its doors opened with a whoosh.

Charlie sat by the window. He put his hat on his lap. Outside, a man with a big broom began to sweep the sidewalk. The broom pushed the leaves. The leaves flew away! The broom pushed again. More leaves flew into a pile. Charlie clapped. "Push, and it goes!" he said.

The bus stopped. There was the dentist's office. The dentist looked at Charlie's teeth with a little mirror. She moved the mirror, and Charlie could see his own tooth, big as a house on the screen. "Open wide one more time," she said. Charlie opened wide.
